messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Insurance Agent
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 39

**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 71-year-old single man who presents for his initial sessions with a cautious, almost formal demeanor. He is a retired insurance agent, a career he describes with a mix of pride and weariness. He lives alone in a modest suburban home, a place he keeps meticulously clean and orderly. He reports that his primary reason for seeking help now, after decades of never speaking to anyone, is a recent, sharp increase in a feeling he calls "the old dread."

The story Mr. A. tells begins not in his childhood home, but in its basement. He is the youngest of three boys, raised by a mother who was emotionally distant and a father who worked long hours. His primary caregiver was an older aunt, a woman who moved in to "help" after his mother’s health declined when he was six. For the next four years, this aunt was the source of his daily torment. He describes the abuse not as explosive rage, but as a cold, systematic process. She would find reasons – a dropped spoon, a missed chore, a "disrespectful" look – and then take him to the basement. There, she would use a wooden yardstick or a leather belt, striking him on his back and legs. He learned to stand perfectly still, to make no sound, because crying only prolonged the punishment. The worst part, he says, was not the pain, but the silence that followed. She would leave him in the dark basement for an hour or more, and he would sit, heart pounding, listening for her footsteps on the stairs.

He never told anyone. He believed it was normal. He believed he was bad.

As an adult, Mr. A. channeled his hypervigilance into his work. As an insurance agent, he was renowned for his meticulous attention to detail, his ability to spot a single inconsistency in a forty-page policy. He was a "closer," a man who could read a room and know exactly when to push and when to back down. He was successful, but he never felt safe. He never married. He tells the therapist that he had a few "close calls" with women, but he always found a reason to end it. "They wanted me to be... present," he says, frowning. "I don't know how to do that."

In the present, Mr. A. lives a life of rigid routine. He wakes at 5:30 AM every day. He eats the same breakfast. He walks the same two-mile route, always on the same side of the street. He describes a constant, low-grade feeling of being watched. In crowds, he feels a physical pressure in his chest, a sense that he is about to be "found out" and punished. He startles at sudden noises, like a car backfiring or a dropped pan in his own kitchen. He has vivid, recurring nightmares. They are not literal replays of the beatings. Instead, he dreams of being trapped in a dark, endless hallway, hearing footsteps behind him. He always wakes up just before they reach him, drenched in a cold sweat.

His PCL-5 score of 39 reflects this pervasive distress. He endorses moderate to severe symptoms of intrusive memories, avoidance of any reminders of his childhood (he has not spoken to his brothers in decades, and he avoids visiting his hometown), and negative alterations in mood and cognition. He struggles to feel positive emotions. He describes his life as a "long sentence I’m serving." His most prominent symptom is the marked alteration in arousal and reactivity. He is constantly on edge, irritable, and has significant difficulty sleeping, often getting only four or five hours a night.

In session, Mr. A. sits rigidly in his chair, his hands resting flat on his knees. He speaks in a measured, controlled tone, as if recounting a story that happened to someone else. He makes little eye contact. He is here because the "old dread" has become unbearable, a constant companion that makes his retirement feel less like a reward and more like an endless, solitary confinement. He wants to know if there is a way to "turn the volume down." He does not know if he can trust the therapist, but he is tired of being alone in the dark.
